You might think asking an AI chatbot for medical advice is obviously a bad idea, yet hundreds of millions of people do so every week.

In an almost fatal incident (now the subject of litigation), ChatGPT advised a pastor to ignore the symptoms of a pulmonary embolism—a condition with a 30% mortality rate. In fact, the advice ChatGPT provided likely made the condition worse…

AI chatbots are useful in many ways, but using them in place of seeing a doctor is not one of them. Given how often they confidently spout nonsense, it's not even wise to use them in place of a Google search.

Yet even OpenAI's own figures show hundreds of millions of people ask ChatGPT health questions every week. Likewise, an analysis of Microsoft Copilot's search logs found health queries were among the most common categories searched in its mobile app.

If you need any evidence of the potential consequences of relying on chatbots for medical advice, a lawsuit filed by a pastor in Florida provides a sobering example. *The New York Times* reports he is suing OpenAI after ChatGPT told him not to worry about the symptoms of a pulmonary embolism.

ChatGPT advised him to simply rest. It not only told him not to seek medical attention, but staying immobile for an extended period in that situation is the worst possible course of action—I say this from personal experience, having developed a pulmonary embolism myself years ago following a twelve-hour long-haul flight combined with a leg injury, a risk researchers were aware of but failed to communicate to passengers.

When Winters was finally admitted to intensive care, doctors said his symptoms likely indicated a series of pulmonary embolisms, and that sitting still for weeks on ChatGPT's advice had made his condition worse.

Winters was reportedly using GPT-4o at the time, an older ChatGPT model notorious for its sycophantic responses. That may explain references in the response to trusting in God, but regardless of which AI model you use, please don't let it provide your medical advice.
